narrative:
The law school's decision was based on a prediction that you have a 60.5% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. This means that, based on the patterns observed in thousands of past students, the school estimates your chances of passing are only about four in ten. Because this probability crosses the school's threshold for acceptable risk, your application was denied.

Three factors weighed most heavily in this decision, ranked from strongest to weakest influence, and each tells a different story.

Your third-year class rank was the most damaging factor overall. You placed in the 3rd decile, meaning roughly 70% of your classmates finished with stronger grades. Among accepted students, the average decile was nearly 5.8, so your standing is well below what the school typically sees. Your first-year class rank told a similar story: 3rd decile versus an average of around 6.0 among accepted applicants. These two academic rankings, taken together, strongly pushed the prediction toward failure. Poor relative performance in law school is historically one of the most reliable signs that a student will struggle with the bar exam, and these two factors carried the most weight in the model's decision.

Interestingly, your LSAT score worked in your favor. At 46, it is well above the average of roughly 37 among accepted students, and this pushed the prediction toward passing. Your undergraduate GPA of 3.50 also exceeds the typical accepted applicant's 3.23, and your family income and full-time status aligned with the majority of admitted students.

However, your strong entrance exam and GPA could not offset the two weak class ranks. To improve your chances in the future, focus on raising your academic standing through rigorous preparation, possibly pursuing a post-baccalaureate program that demonstrates your ability to rank highly among peers. A stronger class rank record would directly counter what the model found most concerning.
